summary:
Mission Control: Design a Space Mission is an interactive web game that teaches students how real space missions are planned. Players choose a mission (Earth Climate Satellite, Asteroid Scout or Mars Weather Probe). They then build a spacecraft in five guided steps: rocket, instruments, power, antenna and optional protection. Live meters show budget, mass and power as they choose.

When they launch, they pilot five stages: launch, travel, orbit, science and communication. Each stage is a hands-on timing challenge in a 3D scene with sound effects. The outcome comes mainly from the design: too little power slows the instruments, a weak antenna loses data, and a heat shield or backup computer cuts specific risks. Player timing adds only a small bonus (about ±8 points). The results screen gives a 0–100 score and explains what helped, what hurt and what to try next, so a failure teaches rather than punishes.

The game turns trade-offs between cost, weight, power and communication into something students can feel rather than memorize. That way of thinking is central to engineering, and the game needs no account or backend, so it is easy to use in classrooms.
details:
What it does and how it works: Mission Control is a browser game where players plan and fly a space mission. They pick a mission (Earth, Asteroid or Mars), build a spacecraft in five guided steps (rocket, instruments, power, antenna, extras) while watching budget, mass and power meters, then fly five stages in 3D: launch, travel, orbit, science and communication. Simple rules turn design choices into results, such as weak power slowing instruments or a weak antenna losing data. A score from 0 to 100 explains what helped, what hurt and what to try next. Player timing adds only about ±8 points, so design decides most of the outcome.

Benefits: It teaches trade-offs by letting players feel them. It is beginner-friendly, encouraging after failure, free of accounts and installs, and works on desktop and mobile.

Intended impact: To make space engineering approachable and build engineering thinking: working within limits, weighing risk and improving a design. I haven’t tested it with students yet, so this is the goal, not a measured result.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for 3D and the Web Audio API for sound. It was built in a conversation with Claude, and the slides were made with pptxgenjs. Any modern browser is enough hardware.

Creativity: The game has a clear story (choose, build, launch, learn). Procedural 3D planets, a modeled rocket and probe, synthesized sound and a hands-on challenge at each stage give it a mission-control feel. Every part has a benefit and a cost, so there are several valid designs.

Factors considered: The lesson of trade-offs stays central. Rules are fair and always explained, every mission has a winning design and many partial ones, the language is friendly, and it works on phones and has a fallback if 3D isn’t available.
